Security is a first-class goal for Deploy App ("Security and quality first"). This page covers how to report vulnerabilities privately, the supported-versions / design-lifetime expectations, and the CA/trust posture that differs between the legacy and Kubernetes stacks.

Reporting a vulnerability

Do not open a public GitHub issue for a security problem. Report it privately so it can be triaged and fixed before disclosure.

When reporting, include the affected stack and version/tag (and the submodule set for the legacy stack), reproduction steps, and the impact you observed.

Supported versions & design lifetime

A Deploy App deployment is intended to be short-lived. The legacy README states a design lifetime of 1–2 months and warns explicitly against running a single deployment longer:

If you wish to use one deployment for longer than the design lifetime of 1–2 months you can change the following env variables. But do understand that this is not recommended and has security implications.

The relevant knobs are the CFSSL certificate expiries, which default to short windows:

CFSSL_CA_EXPIRY="8800h"            # ~366 days; only if you accept the risk
CFSSL_SIGN_DEFAULT_EXPIRY="8800h"

The README is blunt about the tradeoff: if you extend the lifetime, you take responsibility to go through all Dockerfiles and compositions and apply security updates yourself. The supported, secure path is to stand up a fresh deployment from a current tag rather than nurse an old one. Tearing down with docker compose down -v deletes certificates and all user state — treat that as a full reset, not an upgrade step.

CA and trust posture

Both stacks are mTLS-centric — product integration endpoints authenticate the caller by client certificate (the matrix example rejects any caller whose CN does not match the Rasenmaeher service certificate with 403 Forbidden). How the CA and trust distribution are implemented differs sharply between stacks.

Legacy (Docker Compose)

The internal CA is CFSSL (docker-rasenmaeher-cfssl, the cfssl submodule). Public-facing TLS certificates are obtained via miniwerk (python-rasenmaeher-miniwerk) using Let's Encrypt, configured with MW_LE_EMAIL and MW_LE_TEST, and the CA is named via CFSSL_CA_NAME. Certificate lifetimes are governed by the CFSSL_*_EXPIRY variables above.

Kubernetes (opendefence-platform, alpha)

The k8s stack drops CFSSL and miniwerk entirely. CA and trust are handled by cert-manager + trust-manager with an in-cluster PKI (opendefense-pki):

  • A self-signed ClusterIssuer (opendefense-issuer) signs the root CA, which signs an intermediate CA — a normal cert-manager root/intermediate chain.
  • A trust-manager Bundle (opendefense-bundle) distributes the CA chain to a ConfigMap in every namespace (PEM, plus JKS/PKCS#12 formats for Java/keystore consumers). Notably it sets useDefaultCAs: false for the public-CA portion, with a warning that an unpinned default bundle can change underneath you.
  • Public-facing TLS uses cert-manager ClusterIssuers for Let's Encrypt instead of miniwerk.
  • The core API runs as deployment/opendefense-rmapi in namespace opendefense-system.

Because the two stacks use different CA machinery, do not mix guidance: there is no CFSSL or miniwerk on Kubernetes, and there is no cert-manager/trust-manager on the Compose stack.

Supply-chain scanning

CI enforces dependency and image scanning (see Community & Standards): product repos run Snyk on PRs (snyk-test) and monitor main (snyk-monitor), and the legacy stack runs a Syft + Grype SBOM/scan pipeline that uploads findings to DefectDojo after builds. Threat modeling is part of the operational handover — the Deploy App runbook includes a Threat Model section. See Operate (separate book) for day-2 security operations.
